Bayesian safety signal detection with bssd

Source: vignettes/bssd.Rmd
bssd.Rmd
library(bssd)

Introduction

The safety of a study drug is often monitored while the treatment assignment of an ongoing trial is still blinded. The blinded data show which subjects had an adverse event of special interest, but not their treatment groups. bssd computes the posterior probability that the risk of the event is higher on the study drug than on placebo from such data, with the models examined by Duncan (2026):

  • BDRIBS(1) and BDRIBS(2), the Poisson-based model of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) with the total exposure time or the total time at risk (bdribs_post());
  • EXP_BERN, the exponential Bernoulli mixture model (expbern_post());
  • LL_BERN, the log-logistic Bernoulli mixture model (llbern_post()).

Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018) computed the posterior distributions by Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. bssd computes them by numerical integration, so the results do not depend on a random seed, and they are fast enough for simulation studies of the operating characteristics (sim_oc()). The articles vignette("bdribs1"), vignette("bdribs2"), vignette("expbern") and vignette("llbern") describe each model in detail, with examples, the accuracy of the numerical integration and the comparison with MCMC.

Models

The study drug and placebo are randomized in the ratio \(k:1\). The prior distribution of the placebo parameters is based on historical placebo data with the event rate \(\lambda_{HP}\) and the total patient time \(PT_{HP}\), discounted by the factor \(DF\).

BDRIBS. The number of subjects with the event in the blinded data, \(Y\), follows \[Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\{E \delta (r k + 1) / (k + 1)\},\] where \(E\) is the exposure, \(\delta\) is the event rate on placebo and \(r\) is the rate ratio of the study drug to placebo. The priors are \(\delta \sim \mathrm{Gamma}(\lambda_{HP} PT_{HP} / DF, PT_{HP} / DF)\) with shape and rate parameters, and \(r = p / \{k (1 - p)\}\) with \(p \sim \mathrm{Beta}(a, b)\). BDRIBS(1) uses the total exposure time as \(E\). BDRIBS(2) uses the total time at risk, which leaves out the time after the first occurrence of the event. Both are computed by time_at_risk().

EXP_BERN. Subject \(i\) with the follow-up time \(t_i\) had the event (\(Y_i = 1\)) with the probability \[P(Y_i = 1) = w_p \{1 - \exp(-\lambda_p t_i)\} + w_d \{1 - \exp(-r \lambda_p t_i)\},\] where \(w_p = 1 / (k + 1)\) and \(w_d = k / (k + 1)\). The priors of \(\lambda_p\) and \(r\) are those of \(\delta\) and \(r\) in BDRIBS.

LL_BERN. The exponential distribution is replaced by the log-logistic distribution, \[P(Y_i = 1) = w_p F(t_i; \mu_p, \sigma_p) + w_d F(t_i; \mu_d, \sigma_d), \quad F(t; \mu, \sigma) = 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \exp\{(\log t - \mu) / \sigma\}},\] so that the hazard can change over time (ll_cdf()). The relative risk is the ratio of the cumulative incidences at a time \(t^*\), \(RR(t^*) = F(t^*; \mu_d, \sigma_d) / F(t^*; \mu_p, \sigma_p)\). Duncan (2026) does not state which relative risk is used for this model. ?llbern_post describes this choice and the priors.

A signal is declared when the posterior probability that the relative risk exceeds the critical value \(rr_0\) is larger than a threshold, \(P(RR > rr_0 \mid \mathrm{data}) > \mathrm{cutoff}\). The defaults are \(rr_0 = 1\) and \(\mathrm{cutoff} = 0.95\).

Example with aggregate data

Hypothetical example 2 of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018, Section 4.4) has a 2:1 randomization, a background event rate of 0.011 per patient-year on placebo, and 540 patient-years of blinded exposure. The screening analysis of the article treats the background rate as known, which corresponds to pt_hp = Inf. With the uniform prior for \(p\), the posterior probabilities for 8 and 9 events are

ex2 <- expand.grid(rr0 = c(1, 1.3), y = c(8, 9))
ex2$bssd <- mapply(function(y, rr0) {
  bdribs_post(y = y, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011, pt_hp = Inf,
              p_prior = c(1, 1), rr0 = rr0, details = FALSE)$prob
}, ex2$y, ex2$rr0)
ex2$published <- c(0.622, 0.434, 0.756, 0.584)
knitr::kable(ex2[, c("y", "rr0", "bssd", "published")], digits = 3,
             col.names = c("Events", "rr0", "bssd", "Mukhopadhyay et al."))
Events rr0 bssd Mukhopadhyay et al.
8 1.0 0.619 0.622
8 1.3 0.433 0.434
9 1.0 0.753 0.756
9 1.3 0.580 0.584

The published values were computed by MCMC with the bdribs package, and they differ from the values of bssd by at most 0.004. The print method summarizes the posterior with 9 events:

fit9 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                    pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1))
fit9
#> Model: BDRIBS 
#> Relative risk: rate ratio r of study drug to placebo
#> P(r > 1 | data) = 0.753
#> Signal (posterior probability > 0.95): no
#> Posterior of r: mean 1.522, median 1.438, 95% interval (0.379, 3.143)
fit90 <- bdribs_post(y = 9, exposure = 540, k = 2, lambda_hp = 0.011,
                     pt_hp = Inf, p_prior = c(1, 1), level = 0.90)

The posterior mean of \(r\) is 1.52, and the article reports 1.53. The article gives (0.52, 2.83) as the 95% interval of \(r\). This agrees with the equal-tailed 90% interval, (0.51, 2.82), which level = 0.90 gives, and the equal-tailed 95% interval is (0.38, 3.14).

Example with subject-level data

The following data are simulated with sim_blinded() under the placebo distribution and the largest study drug distribution of scenario 6 in Table 1 of Duncan (2026). The 150 subjects are randomized 1:1, they enter the trial uniformly over 26 weeks, and each subject is followed for up to 104 weeks. The time to the event has a log-logistic distribution with \(\sigma = 0.8\), for which the hazard first increases and then decreases. The cumulative incidence at week 104 is 3.5% on placebo and 18.1% on the study drug. The blinded analysis is at week 117, the third interim analysis in the simulations of the folder reproduce of the installed package.

set.seed(2026)
d <- sim_blinded(n = 150, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 104,
                 analysis_time = 117, dist = "loglogistic",
                 par_p = c(7.3, 0.8), par_d = c(5.85, 0.8))
head(d[, c("id", "entry", "follow_up", "event", "event_time")])
#>   id     entry follow_up event event_time
#> 1  1 14.446685  102.5533     0         NA
#> 2  2  3.150173  104.0000     0         NA
#> 3  3  3.683752  104.0000     0         NA
#> 4  4  3.806313  104.0000     0         NA
#> 5  5  9.020966  104.0000     0         NA
#> 6  6  1.833814  104.0000     0         NA
tar <- time_at_risk(d$follow_up, d$event, d$event_time)
tar
#>     exposure time_at_risk      n_event 
#>     15096.61     14605.76        14.00

The column group of d holds the true treatment group, which the blinded analyses do not use.

The priors follow the simulations in the folder reproduce: a historical placebo group of 75 subjects, the size of the current placebo group, followed for 104 weeks and discounted by \(DF = 2\). For BDRIBS and EXP_BERN, \(\lambda_{HP}\) is the constant hazard per week that gives the placebo incidence at week 104, and \(PT_{HP}\) is in patient-weeks. For LL_BERN, the Gamma priors of \(\mu_p\) and \(\sigma_p\) have the means mu_hp and sigma_hp, and pt_hp divided by df_p sets their precision. The simulations use the historical patient time in patient-years for it.

lambda_hp <- -log(1 - ll_cdf(104, mu = 7.3, sigma = 0.8)) / 104
pt_weeks <- 75 * 104
fits <- list(
  BDRIBS1 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]], exposure = tar[["exposure"]],
                        k = 1, lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks,
                        df = 2, t_star = 104),
  BDRIBS2 = bdribs_post(y = tar[["n_event"]],
                        exposure = tar[["time_at_risk"]], k = 1,
                        lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                        t_star = 104),
  EXP_BERN = expbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1,
                          lambda_hp = lambda_hp, pt_hp = pt_weeks, df = 2,
                          t_star = 104),
  LL_BERN = llbern_post(y = d$event, t = d$follow_up, k = 1, mu_hp = 7.3,
                        sigma_hp = 0.8, pt_hp = pt_weeks / 52, df_p = 2,
                        t_star = 104)
)
res <- do.call(rbind, lapply(fits, summary))
res$model <- names(fits)
knitr::kable(res[, c("model", "prob", "signal", "rr_median", "ip_placebo",
                     "ip_drug", "ip_difference")], digits = 3,
             row.names = FALSE)
model prob signal rr_median ip_placebo ip_drug ip_difference
BDRIBS1 0.791 FALSE 2.879 0.053 0.118 0.065
BDRIBS2 0.805 FALSE 3.031 0.053 0.124 0.071
EXP_BERN 0.820 FALSE 3.243 0.052 0.131 0.079
LL_BERN 0.935 FALSE 4.217 0.041 0.152 0.111 
sig <- res$model[res$signal]

The column prob is \(P(RR > 1 \mid \mathrm{data})\). Models with a signal at the threshold 0.95: none. The relative risk is the rate ratio \(r\) for the BDRIBS and EXP_BERN models and \(RR(104)\) for LL_BERN. The table shows its posterior median, because the posterior mean of \(r\) is infinite for EXP_BERN under the default Beta(0.5, 0.5) prior of \(p\) (see ?expbern_post). The last three columns are the posterior means of the cumulative incidences at week 104 and of their difference. The true values are 0.035, 0.181 and 0.146.

Accuracy of the numerical integration

bdribs_post() integrates over one dimension with stats::integrate(). expbern_post() (two dimensions) and llbern_post() (four dimensions) use Gauss-Legendre and Chebyshev quadrature on a region located by a coarse grid. With control$check = TRUE, the default, they repeat the computation on a finer grid, return the finer result, and report an estimate of the integration error of prob:

vapply(fits[c("EXP_BERN", "LL_BERN")], function(f) f$integration$error,
       numeric(1))
#>     EXP_BERN      LL_BERN 
#> 1.814905e-07 3.733315e-04

The number of nodes can be changed with control. ?llbern_post explains why the error estimate of LL_BERN is twice the difference between the two grids. sim_oc() turns the check off by default to save time.

Operating characteristics

sim_oc() simulates trials with sim_blinded(), applies the selected models at each analysis, and returns the proportion of trials with a signal and the posterior mean of the difference in the cumulative incidence. The example below uses the BDRIBS models with 200 simulated trials to keep the run time short; the column se is the Monte Carlo standard error of prob_signal. The cumulative incidence at week 52 is 10% on placebo and 20% on the study drug, 350 subjects enter over 26 weeks, and the analyses are at weeks 26, 52 and 78.

rate_of <- function(ip, t) -log(1 - ip) / t
design <- list(n = 350, k = 1, accrual = 26, follow_up = 52,
               analysis_time = c(26, 52, 78), dist = "exponential",
               par_p = rate_of(0.10, 52), par_d = rate_of(0.20, 52))
oc <- sim_oc(n_sim = 200, design = design,
             models = c("BDRIBS1", "BDRIBS2"),
             priors = list(bdribs = list(lambda_hp = rate_of(0.10, 52),
                                         pt_hp = 175 * 52, df = 2)),
             t_star = 52, seed = 1)
knitr::kable(oc$summary[, c("analysis_time", "model", "prob_signal", "se",
                            "mean_ip_difference",
                            "mean_observed_difference")],
             digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
analysis_time model prob_signal se mean_ip_difference mean_observed_difference
26 BDRIBS1 0.095 0.021 0.060 0.026
26 BDRIBS2 0.115 0.023 0.067 0.026
52 BDRIBS1 0.050 0.015 0.055 0.071
52 BDRIBS2 0.130 0.024 0.073 0.071
78 BDRIBS1 0.045 0.015 0.054 0.093
78 BDRIBS2 0.120 0.023 0.076 0.093

The true difference in the cumulative incidence at week 52 is 0.1. The column mean_observed_difference is the mean difference between the proportions of subjects with the event in the two groups at the analysis, computed from the true group assignment. The scripts in the folder reproduce (system.file("reproduce", package = "bssd")) run the simulations of Duncan (2026) for all four models with 1000 trials per scenario.

Reproduction and validation

The installed package contains the scripts and the results of the reproduction of published results (folder reproduce) and of the comparison with independent computations (folder validation). Each item is judged as PASS (agreement within the tolerance), EXPLAINED (a difference whose reason is registered), FAIL (a difference without a registered reason) or INFO (no value to compare with). The numbers of items are

file PASS EXPLAINED FAIL INFO
reproduce_Duncan2026.csv 15 6 0 7
reproduce_Duncan2026_prior.csv 23 6 0 0
reproduce_Duncan2026_simulation.csv 14 4 0 113
reproduce_Mukhopadhyay2018.csv 82 4 0 1
validate_bdribs_package.csv 35 0 0 0
validate_convergence.csv 19 0 0 0
validate_jags.csv 24 0 0 3
validate_sim_oc.csv 29 0 0 0

The reproduction covers Table 1, the hypothetical examples and the operating characteristics of Mukhopadhyay et al. (2018), and Table 1, Figure 1 and the simulations of Figures 2 to 10 of Duncan (2026). Many simulation results are INFO, because the article does not report all settings of the simulations and the published values are read from the figures. The validation compares bdribs_post() with the bdribs package, expbern_post() and llbern_post() with MCMC in JAGS, the default integration grids with finer grids and with an independent Python implementation, and sim_oc() with an independent Python simulation. The number of FAIL items is 0. The files README.md and results/SUMMARY.md in each folder describe the scripts, the tolerances and the reasons for the EXPLAINED items.

References

Duncan, B. (2026). Robust safety monitoring and signal detection using alternatives to the standard Poisson distribution. Journal of Biopharmaceutical Statistics, 36(2), 227-244. https://doi.org/10.1080/10543406.2024.2395532

Mukhopadhyay, S., Waterhouse, B., and Hartford, A. (2018). Bayesian detection of potential risk using inference on blinded safety data. Pharmaceutical Statistics, 17(6), 823-834. https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.1898
